title: Spurious spin nutation modes arising from truncated memory effects
authors: Markus Weißenhofer, Ritwik Mondal, M. S. Mrudul, Peter M. Oppeneer
abstract: Spin dynamics is conventionally treated as inertia-free. The inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation (iLLG) extends this with a second-order time derivative, predicting a high-frequency nutational mode that recent experiments have claimed to observe and interpreted as direct evidence for spin inertia. We show that when spin inertia is generated by eliminating additional dynamical degrees of freedom, the resulting exact spin-only description is generally non-Markovian. The iLLG is recovered as the low-frequency, second-order truncation of the underlying memory kernel. Using a minimal spin--cavity model, we show that the exact eigenfrequencies and those obtained via the iLLG differ and that the spin nutation mode predicted by the latter is a truncation-induced high-frequency artifact. This raises a broader question of the applicability of the iLLG obtained from analogous low-frequency truncations, which may likewise generate spurious high-frequency roots. Consequently, agreement of a high-frequency spectral feature with the iLLG nutation frequency does not, by itself, establish a physical nutation mode.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes spin dynamics, comparing the full non-Markovian description with the simplified inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (iLLG) equation. The authors demonstrate that the iLLG is merely a low-frequency truncation of the true dynamics. Consequently, the high-frequency nutation mode predicted by the iLLG is identified as a spurious artifact, cautioning against interpreting such spectral matches as definitive physical evidence.
main_problem: The paper investigates the physical validity of high-frequency 'spin nutation modes' predicted by the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (iLLG) equation, questioning if they are genuine physical excitations or mathematical artifacts.
main_result: The iLLG equation is shown to be a low-frequency, second-order truncation of the true, non-Markovian dynamics, leading to the prediction of spurious, high-frequency roots that do not exist in the exact spectrum.
method: The authors compare the exact dynamics derived from a non-Markovian memory kernel (nM-LLG) against the simplified iLLG approximation by analyzing the frequency spectrum in the context of a minimal spin-cavity model.
model_or_system: The system is a localized atomic spin moment coupled to additional dynamical variables (e.g., bosonic cavity modes), leading to a non-Markovian spin dynamics described by a memory kernel.
key_observables: Frequency spectra ($\omega$) of the coupled system, specifically comparing the iLLG nutation frequency ($\omega_{nut}^{iLLG}$) against the exact spectrum ($\omega_{exact}$).
important_parameters: The coupling strength ($g_c$), the cavity resonance frequency ($\omega_c$), and the memory kernel parameters ($\alpha, \eta$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption being tested is the validity of low-frequency, second-order truncations of memory kernels; the iLLG itself is based on such a truncation.
figures_summary: Figures compare the exact and iLLG spectra, showing the divergence of the iLLG nutation mode and the failure of the iLLG to capture physical phenomena like avoided crossings near resonance.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the full non-Markovian dynamics, derives the iLLG as a low-frequency approximation, and then uses a minimal model to explicitly calculate and compare the resulting frequency spectra, demonstrating the artifactual nature of the iLLG root.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous warning about the pitfalls of approximating memory effects in open quantum dynamics, particularly when dealing with high-frequency spectral features.
